blocks.text: The study is an exploratory, qualitative, comparative multiple-case study based on desk research. It relies on publicly available material, listed by case in the bibliography. Its purpose is to identify recurring patterns in founder financing decisions and the conditions under which they hold, not to estimate the effect of any financing choice on company outcomes.

blocks.html: Cases were limited to fintech and logistics because they place contrasting demands on capital: fintech ranges from asset-light payments to balance-sheet lending, while logistics tends to be asset-intensive and thin-margin. Within that filter, cases were selected purposively to vary region, business model, stage and outcome, and to include at least one company that failed after raising institutional capital. The scaled cases also required a public record of funding rounds and investors; the early-stage cases were chosen for how they designed their capital needs, and their public records are thinner. The selected cases are:

CaseSector and capital story
1 · M-KOPA (Kenya)Fintech, asset financing. Debt-funded assets, equity-funded platform.
2 · MNT-Halan (Egypt)Fintech with logistics roots. Local-currency securitisation, raising through devaluation, 2026 EGX listing.
3 · NALA (Tanzania)Fintech, payments. Pivot before institutional capital; Series A raised while profitable; 2026 credit facility to pre-fund payments.
4 · Sendy (Kenya)Logistics, cautionary case. Asset-light transport marketplace that added fulfilment and supply lines funded largely with equity; closed in 2023.
5 · Moniepoint (Nigeria)Fintech, business payments and banking. Revenue-funded until 2019; licensed microfinance bank; over $280M of equity raised.
6 · Autogirl (Nigeria)Logistics and mobility, peer-to-peer vehicle rentals. Largely revenue-funded since 2019, with car owners financing the fleet; expanded to Ghana in 2024.
7 · Feegor (Nigeria)Logistics and B2B commerce, wholesale sourcing marketplace. Asset-light by design: 3PL partners deliver, fintech partners provide BNPL credit.
8 · LemFi (Nigeria)Fintech, cross-border payments and remittances for the African diaspora in Europe and North America. Equity-funded payments business; added credit products through its 2025 acquisition of Pillar.
9 · Earthbond (Nigeria)Fintech, embedded asset financing (solar credit marketplace). Often tagged “climate tech”, but the business is credit origination for partner lenders.

blocks.text: Each case is assessed on the same seven dimensions where evidence allows. The dimensions are not equally relevant or equally documented for every company; where information is undisclosed, the case says so rather than inferring it. All seven are read through one organising question, who carries the asset and its risk (see the next page).

blocks.html:
DimensionQuestions asked of every case
Funding timingWhen did the founder raise, and why then? What was the business condition, and were raises deliberately delayed or accelerated?
Instrument choiceEquity, debt, grant or blended. How did the mix evolve across stages, and why?
Investor selectionWho did the founder choose to take money from, and who did they turn down? What does the investor mix suggest about the founder’s strategic intent?
Dilution managementHow did founders protect ownership through rounds? What dilution patterns emerge, and how do they compare across geographies?
Follow-on fundingAbility to raise a subsequent round, as a market-validated signal of model quality and investor confidence.
Debt vs. equity decisionsWhen did founders shift between debt and equity, and what triggered the shift?
Decline or delay decisionsDocumented cases where founders rejected capital, delayed a raise or took a smaller round than available, and why.

blocks.text: The seven dimensions are read through one question: who carries the asset and its risk? Timing, instrument choice, dilution and investor selection matter here mainly for how they answer it, as the figure shows. The case write-ups keep the seven headings so that cases can be compared, and each case opener names its answer under “Who carries the asset”.

blocks.caption: How each dimension connects to the organising question. Source: Sections 02 and 07.

blocks.title: Unit of analysis and how the cases are used

blocks.text: The unit of analysis is the company. Each case follows one company’s financing decisions from founding to the latest public information. Where a founder’s earlier venture shaped those decisions, as Vasiti did for Feegor, it is described as background and is not assessed against the framework.

The mix of outcomes is deliberate. The five scaled companies show which structures held up at scale; Sendy shows a structure that did not; Moove is read alongside the cases as a comparator. The three early-stage companies are comparators, not tests of success: their outcomes are open, so they show how founders design around an asset before they can finance it. Funding timing, instrument choice and investor selection apply fully at their stage; dilution, follow-on funding and debt-versus-equity decisions are thinly documented and are reported as such. Currency and treasury are not a separate dimension: they are assessed within instrument choice and debt versus equity, because the currency of a liability matters in relation to the asset it funds, and the framework adds a currency row to its stage guidance (Section 7).

blocks.html:
What readers should not generalise from this sample
  • That a financing choice caused an outcome: the cases show associations, and every outcome also reflects execution, markets and timing.
  • That the scaled companies are typical: they were chosen partly for their strong public records, and only one failure is examined in full.
  • That partner models succeed: the early-stage outcomes are not yet known.
  • That the patterns hold beyond fintech and logistics, or outside Egypt, Kenya, Nigeria, Tanzania and Ghana.

blocks.text: Each case draws on publicly available sources: company announcements and blogs, investor and DFI press releases, listing disclosures where available (notably for MNT-Halan’s EGX offering), founder interviews and commentary published in the press, reporting by outlets such as TechCabal, TechCrunch, Rest of World, Enterprise AM and Techpoint Africa, and funding databases (Crunchbase, Tracxn, Briter, Africa: The Big Deal). Material claims are cited in the text by outlet and date, and sources are listed by case in the bibliography.

The cases distinguish four kinds of statement: documented facts, such as round sizes, investors and dates reported by the company, its investors or regulators; founder-reported explanations, such as why a round was raised or a product line closed, which are attributed to the founder; the authors’ interpretations, signalled by language such as “suggests” or “is consistent with”; and open questions, which are stated as such. Where secondary sources disagree, the case reports the range or the better-sourced figure. Events from mid-2026 onward rely on press reports close to the submission date and may be revised.

The study has five main limitations. First, selection bias: cases were chosen partly for the strength of their public record, which favours companies that raised and announced institutional capital, and only one failed company is examined in full. Second, disclosure is uneven: ownership and dilution are rarely public, debt terms are seldom disclosed, and the early-stage cases rely heavily on founder interviews given to the press. Third, the companies differ widely in maturity, from pre-seed startups to a lender preparing to list, so stage effects and strategy effects are hard to separate. Fourth, the cases span different markets, regulators and currencies, which limits direct comparison. Fifth, applying one framework to businesses as different as a deposit-taking bank, a remittance app and a car-rental marketplace means some dimensions carry more weight in some cases than in others. The findings are therefore patterns and plausible explanations, not estimates of causal effects, and they are not representative of African startups generally.
